sources.note: Issued under s.7 AMLO and s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance; revised May 2023 (the version you supplied).

sources.label: AMLO (Cap. 615)
sources.note: CDD by an agent leaves the bank liable (s.18(6)); duty to keep records and the manner of keeping them (ss.20–21).

drafting: **Legal holds:** the vendor keeps records longer on the bank's instruction and never deletes them during a hold.
**Tipping-off:** bind vendors that see alerts, case files or report information to confidentiality covering suspicions, since disclosing them can be an offence (7.6).
**Exit:** all CDD and screening records handed back in usable form before the vendor stops.

terms.title: Relying on an intermediary for CDD
terms.summary: Reliance is a separate regime: a regulated intermediary performs part of CDD with its own procedures, and the bank should obtain confirmations and undertakings that secure access to what it collected (4.11.3–4.11.5). The bank keeps ultimate responsibility (4.11.1).
require: **Eligible intermediary:** only the categories in AMLO Sch. 2 s.18(3) qualify, and the bank must take appropriate measures to confirm the intermediary meets the criteria (4.11.8–4.11.14).
**Written confirmation:** the intermediary agrees to act as the bank's intermediary and states which CDD measures it will perform (4.11.3(a)).
**Data straight away:** the bank obtains the data or information immediately after each CDD measure; copies of documents can follow (4.11.4).
**Documents on request:** copies of documents and records provided on request without delay, throughout the record-keeping period (4.11.3(b), 4.11.5).

**Retention undertaking:** where the intermediary keeps the documents and records, an undertaking to keep all underlying CDD information for the whole relationship and at least five years after it ends, or for any longer period the HKMA specifies (4.11.5).
**On exit or failure:** hand over all CDD information if the intermediary is about to cease trading or stops acting for the bank (4.11.5, 4.11.7, 8.12).
**Ongoing monitoring stays with the bank:** reliance does not cover it (4.11.1, footnote 48).
**Record-keeping systems:** the intermediary has systems to comply with all AMLO and Guideline record-keeping requirements (8.10).
**Doubts:** if the bank doubts the intermediary's reliability, it reviews the intermediary's ability to perform CDD and redoes doubtful CDD as soon as reasonably practicable (4.11.7).

sources.label: AMLO (Cap. 615)
sources.note: Conditions for carrying out CDD by means of intermediaries.

drafting: **Test it:** the bank should sample-test that documents arrive on demand without undue delay (4.11.6); give it the right to.

terms.title: Debt collection agencies
terms.summary: The Code of Banking Practice sets detailed, prescriptive terms for collection agencies, and the bank remains accountable to customers for complaints about the agency and should not disclaim responsibility for its misconduct (CoBP 46.5).
require: **Formal contract:** a formal contractual relationship, with the contract or written instructions requiring collectors to observe the conduct rules in 46.1 to 46.3 (46.4).

**Conduct:** act within the law, avoid anything prejudicial to the bank's business, integrity, reputation or goodwill, and keep a strict duty of confidentiality over customer information (46.1). Never use intimidation or violence ('must not'), and do not use harassment or improper tactics such as posters, persistent calls or electronic messages, calls at unreasonable hours, pestering referees, family or friends, false names, anonymous calls or notes, abusive or threatening remarks, or false or misleading representations (46.2).
**Third parties:** no attempt to recover from referees, family or friends who have not formally guaranteed the debt, by written instruction or contract clause (46.3).
**Principal and agent:** the contract states the relationship is principal and agent, and prohibits sub-contracting the collection to anyone else (46.5).
**Identification:** collectors identify themselves and the bank, and carry authorization documents without account details (46.10).
**Records:** customers told that calls are recorded and why; records of other contacts kept; recordings and contact records kept at least 30 days (47.5).

**Limits:** no authority to start legal proceedings without the bank's formal approval (47.9); no free hand on recovery procedures (47.3); all recovery stops immediately once the debt is settled in full (46.11), and once the bank learns of a bankruptcy order against the debtor (46.13).

**Data privacy:** clauses protecting customer information and barring sharing with anyone else, including other agencies (CoBP 47.11). An agency handling customer data only on the bank's behalf will usually be a data processor (counsel's view), so the bank must also adopt contractual or other means against excessive retention and unauthorized or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use (PDPO DPP2(3), DPP4(2)); see the data processor clause.

sources.label: HKMA Guideline 3.4.1 Debt Collection Agencies
sources.note: Letter of 3 May 1996: no intimidation or violence, and no recovery from non-guarantor third parties, given to agencies in writing.

sources.label: PDPO (Cap. 486)
sources.note: An agent's acts done with the bank's authority are treated as done by the bank as well as by the agent, for PDPO purposes other than criminal proceedings; this attributes liability and does not itself require any clause.

drafting: **Oversight rights:** unscheduled visits to check professionalism, integrity, training, resourcing and compliance (47.6); a duty to take remedial action on complaints (47.7); termination for unacceptable practices or breach (47.12).

**Selection file:** company search identifying owners and directors, a basic assessment of financial soundness, a site visit, an evaluation of operations and, for a new agency, references from at least two existing clients (preferably authorized institutions), with the procedures regularly reviewed (47.1).

**Data minimisation:** do not pass information about referees or any third party other than debtors and guarantors to the agency; if a referee must be approached to locate the debtor or guarantor, the bank's own staff do it without causing nuisance (46.7).

terms.title: Marketing and distribution partners
terms.summary: Partners who promote the bank's products, run its digital channels or sell third-party products through it expose the bank to Code and PDPO duties that the contract has to carry.
require: **Fair promotion:** the bank is responsible for ensuring that the promotional activities and materials its engaged or collaborating partners publish or share during the engagement are fair and reasonable, not misleading, and compliant with CoBP 11.2, 11.4 and 11.6 (11.7). Approval, take-down and control rights over partner materials follow from this (drafting inference).
**Records:** proper records of digital marketing materials and communications kept for a reasonable period, and not left to the channel provider unless the contract provides for it (11.5).

**Agents' conduct:** authorized agents should have as an objective to work in customers' best interests and endeavour to avoid conflicts; where a conflict cannot be avoided they should disclose it, manage it or decline the business; and, where appropriate, their remuneration should encourage responsible conduct and fair treatment and avoid conflicts (2.5, a general principle).

**Third-party products:** the bank's own duties on terms and conditions (making them available, answering queries, advising customers to read them and allowing time to review: 5.1, 5.8) apply to third-party products too; the provider is told of the rest of section 5 and asked to observe it as far as possible (5.15). The agreement clearly defines each party's responsibilities for handling disputes, and lets the bank obtain the information it needs to help customers in dispute resolution (11.14).

sources.label: PDPO (Cap. 486)
sources.note: Using customers' data in direct marketing needs prescribed notice and consent (ss.35C, 35E); providing it to another person for that person's direct marketing needs written notice and written consent (ss.35J–35K).

drafting: **Data flows:** decide whether the partner processes data only for the bank (a data processor: the bank needs contractual or other means under DPP2(3) and DPP4(2), and if the partner markets to the bank's customers, that is the bank's own use in direct marketing and needs notice and consent under PDPO ss.35C and 35E) or for its own marketing (a provision of data needing written notice and written consent under ss.35J–35K). Name partners such as co-branding or loyalty-programme providers specifically in customer notices (CoBP 8.3), and draft accordingly.

process.heading: Before you sign
process.lede: Most of the regulatory exposure is created, or avoided, before the contract exists.
points: **Risk assessment:** the board and management should ensure that a comprehensive assessment of operational, legal and reputation risks has been made, covering among other things the importance and criticality of the service, the reasons for outsourcing and the effect on the bank's risk profile, and that every risk identified is adequately addressed before launch (SA-2 2.2.1).

**Due diligence:** beyond cost and quality, the vendor's financial soundness, reputation, managerial skills, technical and operational capability and capacity, cultural fit, familiarity with banking and capacity to keep pace with innovation (SA-2 2.3.1).

**Critical technology services:** commission a detailed assessment of the provider's IT control environment, ideally by a party independent of the provider, and give the report to the HKMA (TM-G-1 7.1.1).
**Critical operations:** verify the vendor's operational resilience is at least equivalent to the bank's own (OR-2 6.2, consultation draft).

**Talk to the HKMA:** discuss the plan with the HKMA in advance before outsourcing in any banking-related area (back-office included) or changing the scope of an arrangement, and satisfy it that the section 2 issues are addressed; ask the HKMA if unsure whether an activity is in scope (SA-2 1.3.2). A digital bank should also demonstrate that SA-2 will be complied with (Digital Bank Guideline para 23).

**Overseas:** understand the country risk; generally obtain a legal opinion from a reputable firm in that jurisdiction on foreign authorities' access to customer data, and assess how likely that access is; do not outsource to a jurisdiction that is inadequately regulated or whose secrecy laws may hamper access by the HKMA or the external auditors; and have the HKMA's right of access confirmed in writing by the bank and its home or host authority (SA-2 2.9.1). A locally incorporated bank sending a major part of its data processing offshore is expected to keep a robust, documented and tested back-up system and contingency plan in an acceptable jurisdiction (SA-2 2.9.2).

**Customers:** tell customers in general terms that their data may be outsourced, and give specific notice of significant initiatives, especially overseas ones (SA-2 2.5.3). For overseas outsourcing, generally tell them the country where the provider is located (and any later change) and any right of access the overseas authorities have (2.9.1). The Code expects customers to be told, on or before collection, that data may go to data processors and debt collection agencies (CoBP 8.3).

**Data handling:** when personal data goes to a service provider, satisfy yourself that it will be kept confidential and adequately safeguarded, and adopt contractual or other means against unauthorized or accidental access, processing, use, erasure or loss and against keeping it longer than the agreement's purposes need; the bank stays accountable to customers and should not disclaim responsibility for the provider's breaches (CoBP 8.8; see also PDPO DPP2(3), DPP4(2)).
process.takeaway: Keep a dated file for each arrangement showing the risk assessment, due diligence, HKMA discussion and approvals (counsel's practice suggestion): the HKMA will check in examinations, off-site reviews and prudential interviews whether the section 2 concerns were addressed (SA-2 1.3.6).

process.heading: During the contract
points: **Monitoring:** effective procedures to monitor performance, manage the relationship and manage the risks, run by staff with the right expertise (SA-2 2.6.1, 2.6.3).

**Review cycle:** re-perform the risk assessment regularly (SA-2 2.2.2); review the agreement against market standards and strategy regularly, for example annually (2.4.2); and confirm the adequacy of each critical technology provider's IT control environment every year (TM-G-1 7.1.1).
**Internal audit:** regular review of the controls over the arrangement (SA-2 2.6.5).
**Concentration:** try to avoid placing excessive reliance on a single provider for critical technology services (TM-G-1 7.1.1).
**Mapping:** update the mapping of dependencies behind critical operations at least annually and after material changes (OR-2 5.4, consultation draft).

**Escalation and resilience:** reporting procedures that promptly escalate problems to the bank's and the provider's management (SA-2 2.6.4); for vendors supporting critical operations, arrangements to keep satisfying the bank that the vendor maintains an acceptable level of operational resilience (OR-2 6.2, consultation draft).

process.heading: When it goes wrong
points: **Fix it:** take appropriate action to rectify deficiencies; in extreme cases the HKMA can require alternative arrangements (SA-2 1.3.5).

**Have a way out:** keep a contingency plan for critical outsourced technology services that covers the provider's unavailability, including insolvency, and which may include an exit management plan and identified alternative providers (TM-G-1 7.1.1); in building it, consider whether alternative providers are available or the activity could come back in-house, and at what cost, time and resources (SA-2 2.7.3). For critical operations, OR-2 6.2 (consultation draft) also expects exit strategies.

**Do not continue a weakening arrangement:** an arrangement that may compromise or weaken internal controls or business conduct (SA-2 1.2.2), or weaken the operational resilience of critical operations (OR-2 6.2, consultation draft), should not be entered into or continued.

title: AML, sanctions & fraud
oneLiner: Remote onboarding, mule accounts and suspicious-transaction reporting are where a digital bank and its staff carry criminal and regulatory risk.
keyPoints: Financial crime is the area most likely to put the bank, and its staff personally, on the wrong side of a criminal statute. Three regimes interlock.
**AMLO (Cap. 615):** imposes [[customer due diligence|CDD]], ongoing monitoring and record-keeping duties; the HKMA enforces them through disciplinary powers.

**OSCO, DTROP, UNATMO:** These proceeds-of-crime and terrorist-financing laws make dealing with tainted property an offence, and require a [[suspicious transaction report|STR]] whenever staff know or suspect.
**Sanctions law:** prohibits making funds available to designated persons.
**Scams:** On top of this sits Hong Kong's scam problem. [[Mule|money mule]] accounts are how fraud proceeds move, and the HKMA now treats anti-fraud as a core supervisory priority.
A bank that never meets its customers face to face runs almost all of these controls in software, so counsel needs to understand how that software works.

deepDive.heading: Schedule 2 and remote onboarding
points: **Timing:** Under AMLO Schedule 2, CDD must normally be completed before the relationship begins (s.3), and ongoing monitoring keeps it current (s.5).
**Remote onboarding:** Every customer of a digital bank is onboarded remotely, so s.9 is the section that shapes your onboarding design.
**s.9(1):** Where a customer is not physically present for identification, the bank must take at least one of three extra measures.
**Re-verify:** verify identity again using documents or data not already used.
**Supplement:** take supplementary verification measures.
**First payment:** make sure the first payment comes from an account in the customer's name at an authorized institution (or an equivalent regulated institution).
**s.9(2):** disapplies s.9(1) where identity was verified using data from a recognized digital identification system such as iAM Smart.

visual.caption: Customer not physically present (AMLO Sch. 2 s.9(1)): take at least one of these. Under s.9(2) none is needed where identity was verified through a recognized digital identification system such as iAM Smart.

items.note: Verify identity again using documents or data not already used

items.label: Supplement
items.note: Take supplementary verification measures

items.label: First payment

deepDive.heading: eKYC and deepfakes
deepDive.lede: App-based document-and-selfie eKYC remains lawful, but it must achieve the HKMA's two outcomes.
points: **Identity authentication:** the document is genuine.
**Identity matching:** the applicant is its holder.
**Replacement circular:** A September 2026 HKMA circular is reported to have replaced the 2019 and 2021 remote on-boarding circulars.
**Deepfakes and recalibration:** It targets deepfakes and expects banks to keep recalibrating their solutions rather than sign them off once.
**Verify:** Confirm its terms on the HKMA site.

deepDive.heading: Guideline and enforcement
deepDive.lede: The HKMA AML/CFT Guideline (revised May 2023) is issued under AMLO s.7 and BO s.7(3), and its 'must' and 'should' provisions are mandatory (para 1.6).
points: **Disciplinary trigger:** Breaching it does not by itself make anyone liable to proceedings, but it is admissible in AMLO court proceedings, the HKMA must have regard to it in deciding whether Schedule 2 was breached, and a Schedule 2 contravention triggers the s.21 disciplinary power (paras 1.7–1.8).
**Recent penalties:** Hua Nan HK$9m and DBS HK$10m in 2024, and Indian Overseas Bank HK$8.5m in 2025.
**Common failures:** Each concerned failures in monitoring or record-keeping that ran for years.
deepDive.takeaway: They were systemic control gaps, not one bad customer.

deepDive.heading: Suspicion reporting
deepDive.lede: Reporting is a personal duty under the criminal law.
points: **Duty to report:** Under s.25A of OSCO and DTROP, and s.12 of UNATMO, knowledge or suspicion must be reported to the [[JFIU]] as soon as reasonable.
**Separate offence:** [[tipping-off|Tipping-off]] is a separate offence.
**JFIU reply:** The JFIU may reply with a [[letter of no consent]].
**Freeze decisions:** Tam Sze Leung v Commissioner of Police [2024] HKCFA 8 upheld that regime but treated the decision to freeze as the bank's own, so record your reasoning.

deepDive.heading: Sanctions regime
deepDive.lede: Hong Kong gives legal effect only to UN sanctions, through regulations under Cap. 537 and, for terrorist designations, UNATMO.
points: **Foreign lists:** Other countries' lists have no legal force here.
**Policy screening:** Correspondent banking and card-scheme exposure still lead most banks to screen against them as a matter of policy.
deepDive.takeaway: That policy should rest on the contract with the customer.

deepDive.heading: Information sharing under Part XIIAA
deepDive.lede: The Banking (Amendment) Ordinance 2025 came into force on 3 November 2025 and added Part XIIAA to the BO.
points: **Safe harbour:** Part XIIAA protects sharing of account information with other AIs through HKMA-designated platforms such as [[FINEST]].
**Conditions:** The protection depends on good faith, reasonable care, and limits on purpose and confidentiality.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Customer due diligence: what it is and when it applies
provisions.summary: Section 2 of Schedule 2 defines the CDD measures: identify and verify the customer and any beneficial owner, understand the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship, and verify anyone who claims to act for the customer. Section 3 sets when the measures must be carried out, including before a business relationship is established, when money laundering or terrorist financing is suspected, and when there is doubt about data obtained earlier.
provisions.counselNote: These are 'specified provisions'. A contravention can lead to HKMA disciplinary action under s.21 and, where knowing, to criminal liability under s.5. In legal terms, your onboarding journey is how the bank carries out s.2.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Customer not physically present for identification
provisions.summary: Where the customer is not physically present for identification, s.9(1) requires at least one of three measures: further verification using documents, data or information not previously used; supplementary measures to verify the information obtained; or ensuring the first payment is made through an account in the customer's name with an authorized institution (or an equivalent regulated institution). Since the 2022 amendments took effect on 1 June 2023, s.9(2) disapplies this requirement where identity is verified using data from a recognised digital identification system (iAM Smart is the recognised example).
provisions.counselNote: This section shapes a digital bank's onboarding design. The iAM Smart route removes the s.9(1) requirement. Any other eKYC route needs a documented set of compensating measures and must meet the HKMA's remote onboarding expectations.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Ongoing monitoring
provisions.summary: Institutions must monitor business relationships continuously. That means keeping CDD information up to date, scrutinising transactions for consistency with what the bank knows of the customer and its risk profile, and identifying complex, unusually large or unusual patterns of transactions that have no apparent economic or lawful purpose.
provisions.counselNote: Failures in transaction monitoring are the most common theme in HKMA AMLO enforcement. Your monitoring rules, thresholds and alert backlog are therefore legal exposure, not only an operational matter.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Record keeping
provisions.summary: Institutions must keep CDD records (identification data, account files and business correspondence) and transaction records. Retention is generally at least five years after the business relationship ends or the transaction is completed, and records must be retrievable without undue delay.
provisions.counselNote: The DBS action in 2024 included record-keeping failures. Retention design has to cover eKYC evidence such as images, liveness results and device data, and must survive changes of vendor and app version.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: HKMA disciplinary powers and pecuniary penalties
provisions.summary: Where an institution contravenes a specified provision, the HKMA, as relevant authority for AIs, may publicly reprimand it, order remedial action, and impose a pecuniary penalty of up to HK$10 million or three times the profit gained or costs avoided, whichever is greater. The HKMA has published a guideline on how it exercises the penalty power.
provisions.counselNote: Confirmed recent actions: Hua Nan Commercial Bank, Hong Kong branch, HK$9m (April 2024); DBS Bank (Hong Kong) HK$10m (July 2024); Indian Overseas Bank, Hong Kong branch, HK$8.5m (July 2025), with a remedial order and a look-back review. Remediation and cooperation affect the outcome.

provisions.title: Duty to report suspicion; tipping-off
provisions.summary: A person who knows or suspects that property is the proceeds of, or was used or is intended for use in connection with, an indictable offence must disclose this to an authorised officer (in practice the JFIU) as soon as reasonable. Disclosure gives a defence to the s.25 money laundering offence. Failing to disclose and tipping-off are separate offences. Section 25A of DTROP (Cap. 405) and s.12 of UNATMO (Cap. 575) impose parallel duties for drug proceeds and terrorist property.
provisions.counselNote: The duty falls on individual employees as well as the bank. Staff are protected when they report internally under the employer's procedures, so the escalation route to the MLRO must be written down, trained and auditable.

provisions.title: Implementing UN Security Council sanctions
provisions.summary: Section 3 empowers the Chief Executive to make regulations implementing UN Security Council sanctions. The country-specific regulations typically prohibit making funds or economic resources available to designated persons, subject to licences. Terrorist designations are handled separately under UNATMO (Cap. 575).
provisions.counselNote: UN sanctions are the only sanctions with legal force in Hong Kong. The bank's screening of US, EU or UK lists is a matter of policy and risk appetite and needs a contractual basis in the customer terms.

provisions.instrument: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions)
provisions.ref: Revised May 2023 (effective 1 June 2023 per the HKMA issuing circular)
provisions.title: HKMA's detailed AML/CFT expectations
provisions.summary: Issued under AMLO s.7 and BO s.7(3), the Guideline explains how the HKMA expects AIs to meet Schedule 2. It covers the risk-based approach, institutional risk assessment, CDD, ongoing monitoring, screening, suspicious transaction reporting and record keeping. The 2023 revision reflected the AMLO amendments that took effect on 1 June 2023.
provisions.counselNote: Its 'must' and 'should' provisions are mandatory (para 1.6). Breach is not by itself actionable, but the Guideline is admissible in AMLO proceedings, the HKMA must have regard to it, and non-compliance can count against the Seventh Schedule criteria (paras 1.7–1.8). Map each paragraph to a policy, a named control owner and the evidence that the control works.

provisions.title: Remote on-boarding of individual customers (updated for deepfake risk)
provisions.summary: Addressed to AIs and SVF licensees, this circular supersedes the circulars of 1 February 2019 and 24 May 2021 (iAM Smart). It restates two principles: identity authentication (the identity document and data are genuine) and identity matching (the applicant is the true holder). It also expects remote onboarding solutions to be recalibrated on an ongoing basis against deepfake and impersonation risk.
provisions.counselNote: This is now the main supervisory text for your onboarding design. Check whether your vendor contracts and model governance allow the bank to recalibrate quickly.

provisions.instrument: Banking Ordinance (Cap. 155), as amended by the Banking (Amendment) Ordinance 2025 (Ord. No. 23 of 2025)
provisions.title: Sharing of information among authorized institutions
provisions.summary: In force from 3 November 2025, Part XIIAA lets AIs voluntarily share customer account information with each other through HKMA-designated platforms, for the purpose of detecting or preventing money laundering, terrorist or proliferation financing and related crime such as fraud. It gives a statutory safe harbour on condition of good faith, reasonable care, use restrictions and confidentiality.
provisions.counselNote: This finally lets banks share data on individual (not only corporate) mule accounts through FINEST. Each disclosure must stay within the statutory purpose and conditions, and must be logged.

checklist: **Build a control matrix** that maps every AMLO Schedule 2 obligation and Guideline section to a named owner, a system control and the evidence it produces.

**Review the eKYC solution** against the HKMA's current remote on-boarding circular (reported as reissued in September 2026), and document how it detects deepfakes, injection attacks and impersonation, and how often it is recalibrated.
**Approve STR escalation procedures** and wording for customer communications (app messages, chatbot scripts, call-centre scripts) that cannot amount to tipping-off.

**Adopt a written policy on freezing accounts** and handling letters of no consent that reflects Tam Sze Leung [2024] HKCFA 8, including periodic review of frozen balances and how customers can challenge a freeze.
**Set the sanctions policy**: UN and UNATMO designations as the legal minimum, other lists as risk appetite, with matching rights to refuse, suspend and terminate in the customer terms.
**Put Part XIIAA sharing procedures in place**: purpose check, data minimisation, approval, logging and confidentiality, aligned with PDPO obligations.
**Benchmark monitoring and record keeping** against the published HKMA s.21 enforcement statements, and brief the board on gaps.
itAngle: **Mapping eKYC:** Map the eKYC stack to the legal tests. Document authenticity checks deliver identity authentication. Face match, liveness and virtual-camera or emulator detection deliver identity matching. Keep the evidence long enough to satisfy the Schedule 2 record-keeping rules.

**Models as controls:** Transaction monitoring rules and ML models are legal controls. Keep version control, tuning rationale, validation reports and alert-backlog metrics, because the HKMA asks why a threshold was set where it was.

**Mule signals:** Device binding and graph analytics (one device or IP linked to many accounts, rapid pass-through flows) are the main mule signals. FINEST under Part XIIAA works like a threat-intelligence feed with statutory conditions attached.

**Neutral responses:** Prevent tipping-off in the system itself: error codes, push notifications, API responses and chatbot replies on restricted accounts must be neutral, and STR case data must sit behind role-based access.

**Fuzzy matching:** Sanctions screening quality depends on fuzzy matching (including Chinese names and their romanisation), how quickly list updates are applied, and real-time screening of instant FPS payments.
virtualBankNotes: **Non-face-to-face book:** The whole customer book is non-face-to-face, so AMLO Sch. 2 s.9 bites on every customer who is not identified through iAM Smart or another recognized digital identification system (s.9(2)). The choice between the iAM Smart route and document-and-selfie eKYC therefore has direct legal consequences.

**Mule recruiters:** Fast app-based onboarding at scale attracts mule recruiters. Expect HKMA scrutiny of early-life account monitoring, limits on new accounts, and participation in FINEST and the Suspicious Account Alert.

**Device controls:** Device binding and controls that detect one device used for many accounts do the job branch staff do elsewhere. Document them as AML/fraud controls, not just as IT security features.

**Anti-scam measures:** Industry anti-scam measures for retail banks, such as Money Safe under the HKMA's December 2024 customer-empowerment circular, are also expected of digital banks. Any step that assumes an in-person visit needs a robust remote equivalent.
pitfalls: **Vendor certifications:** Treating an eKYC vendor's certifications as regulatory approval. The HKMA does not approve vendors. The bank owns the risk assessment and must keep recalibrating the solution.
**Freeze communications:** Tipping off a customer through automated freeze notices, chatbot answers or frontline staff explaining a restriction.

**STR filing:** Waiting until an internal investigation is finished before filing an STR (the test is 'as soon as reasonable'), or filing defensively without analysis, which weakens both the reports and the bank's defence.
**Foreign sanctions:** Telling customers that US or EU sanctions are Hong Kong legal requirements, or ignoring them where correspondent or card-scheme contracts make them binding in practice.

glossary.definition: Customer due diligence: identifying and verifying the customer and any beneficial owner, understanding the purpose of the relationship, and verifying anyone acting for the customer (AMLO Sch. 2 s.2).
Suspicious transaction report: the disclosure made to the JFIU under s.25A of OSCO or DTROP, or s.12 of UNATMO, when someone knows or suspects that property is criminal or terrorist property.
Joint Financial Intelligence Unit, Hong Kong's financial intelligence unit. It is run jointly by the Hong Kong Police Force and the Customs and Excise Department, and it receives and analyses STRs.
The offence of disclosing information likely to prejudice an investigation, knowing or suspecting that a suspicious transaction report has been made.

A JFIU reply to an STR saying it does not consent to the reported dealing. Banks usually respond by freezing the funds. The Court of Final Appeal upheld the regime in Tam Sze Leung v Commissioner of Police [2024] HKCFA 8.
A person whose bank account receives and passes on fraud or other criminal proceeds, knowingly or not. Mule accounts are often opened, sold or rented specifically for this purpose.
Financial Intelligence Evaluation Sharing Tool, the bank-to-bank platform launched by the HKMA, HKAB and the Police on 20 June 2023 for sharing information on suspected fraud and mule networks.
The Hong Kong Police anti-fraud search engine (CyberDefender). Its 'high risk' data drives the banks' Suspicious Account Alert on payments.

title: Customers & conduct
oneLiner: App-only banks must deliver codes, disclosures, consent and complaint rights through screens and logs, and the HKMA tests outcomes.
keyPoints: Conduct rules govern how a bank treats retail customers once they have signed up. In Hong Kong very little of this sits in the Banking Ordinance itself; it comes from several layers instead.

**Code and Charter:** The industry [[Code of Banking Practice]] is voluntary on paper, but the HKMA monitors compliance with it as if it were binding, and adds its [[Treat Customers Fairly|TCF]] Charter and conduct circulars.
**Statute and common law:** Statute covers deposit protection (Cap. 581), personal data (Cap. 486) and unfair terms (Caps. 71 and 458); the common law adds a duty of confidentiality.
**Investment and insurance:** Once the bank sells these products, the SFC and Insurance Authority regimes apply, with the HKMA as frontline supervisor.
**Disputes:** Monetary disputes the bank cannot resolve can go to the [[FDRC]].
An app-only bank has no branch staff or paper to rely on, so it must meet every one of these obligations through screens, notifications and logs.

deepDive.heading: Code of Banking Practice
deepDive.lede: Treat the Code of Banking Practice as quasi-regulation.
points: **HKMA endorsement:** It describes itself as voluntary, but the HKMA endorses it, expects compliance and checks it in supervision.
**Breach detection:** Breaches come to light through complaints, FDRC cases and conduct reviews.
**Current revision:** took effect on 7 December 2023, with phased deadlines for system changes.

deepDive.heading: Unauthorised e-banking transactions
deepDive.lede: For an app-only bank, the Code's most important rule concerns unauthorised e-banking transactions.
points: **Customer liability:** The customer bears no direct loss from unauthorised e-banking transactions unless they acted fraudulently or with gross negligence, or failed to report a compromised, lost or stolen device or credential as soon as reasonably practicable (CoBP s.51). Knowingly letting others use a device or credentials may be gross negligence; card transactions follow s.39 instead.
**Evidence:** The HKMA has told card issuers to get adequate evidence before blaming a loss on the customer, so 'the OTP was entered correctly' is not enough on its own.
**Contract terms:** The terms and conditions will not rescue the bank either.
**CECO:** subjects exclusion clauses to a reasonableness test.
**HKMA review:** The HKMA also reads the terms against the Code.

deepDive.heading: Deposit Protection Scheme
deepDive.lede: The [[Deposit Protection Scheme|DPS]] is statutory and detailed.
points: **Limit:** Since 1 October 2024 the limit is HK$800,000 per depositor per bank.
**Signage:** Since 1 January 2025 members must display the membership sign on e-banking platforms.
**Disclosures:** Statements about whether a product is protected, and the [[negative disclosure]] required for unprotected products, are prescribed in detail.

deepDive.heading: Confidentiality and data
deepDive.lede: Confidentiality has two sources: the [[Tournier duty]] (Hong Kong has no general statutory bank-secrecy provision) and the PDPO.
points: **Lawful disclosures:** Disclosures to the JFIU, to other AIs under BO Part XIIAA, and to credit reference agencies under the Consumer Credit Data Code are each lawful only within their own limits.
**Direct marketing:** PDPO Part 6A requires notice and consent before use and is backed by criminal sanctions.
deepDive.takeaway: Consent flags must therefore actually control what the marketing engine sends.

deepDive.heading: Product sales and digital banks
points: **Investments:** Selling investments makes the bank an SFC [[registered institution]], supervised day to day by the HKMA.
**Suitability:** The suitability obligation in the SFC Code of Conduct then applies, and selling online does not weaken it.
**Insurance:** Selling insurance needs a licence from the Insurance Authority.
**Digital banks:** carry extra expectations. The digital bank guideline rules out minimum account balance requirements and low-balance fees (para 6).
**Complaint channels:** Digital banks' complaint channels must also work without branches.

provisions.instrument: Code of Banking Practice (HKAB/DTCA, endorsed by the HKMA)
provisions.title: Retail banking standards; liability for unauthorised e-banking transactions
provisions.summary: A non-statutory industry code that sets standards on disclosure, fees and charges, account operation, cards, e-banking, complaints and customer information. A customer should not bear direct loss from unauthorised e-banking transactions unless they acted fraudulently or with gross negligence. Customers may also be liable for all losses if they acted with gross negligence (which may include knowingly letting others use their device or credentials) or failed to report a compromised, lost or stolen device or credential as soon as reasonably practicable (s.51.2). Card transactions follow s.39 instead. The 2023 revision added protections for digital banking and gave customers more control over their accounts.
provisions.counselNote: The HKMA expects every AI to comply and monitors compliance in supervision. Treat it as binding, and check that the terms and conditions, refund decisions and app journeys all match it.

provisions.title: Fair treatment principles
provisions.summary: Five high-level principles for the fair treatment of retail customers, drawing on the G20 High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection. All 22 retail banks signed it at launch. It complements rather than replaces existing law, and the HKMA expects boards and senior management to embed it.
provisions.counselNote: The HKMA tests outcomes (product design, pricing, complaints handling) as well as compliance with rules. Check whether your bank has signed; the HKMA encourages all AIs to follow the principles either way.

provisions.instrument: Financial Dispute Resolution Scheme (FDRC Terms of Reference)
provisions.ref: Terms of Reference as enhanced from 1 Jan 2018
provisions.title: Out-of-court resolution of monetary disputes
provisions.summary: Eligible claimants (individuals, sole proprietors and, since mid-2018, small enterprises) may bring monetary claims against member financial institutions. Claims are handled through mediation first and then arbitration. The 2018 enhancements raised the maximum claim from HK$500,000 to HK$1 million and the time limit from 12 to 24 months. Larger claims can be handled if both parties consent.
provisions.counselNote: AIs are expected to be FDRC members. The customer normally has to complain to the bank first, so final-response letters and in-app messages should point the customer to the FDRC and HKMA routes.

provisions.title: Statutory deposit protection
provisions.summary: Licensed banks are Scheme members unless exempted, and pay levies into the DPS Fund administered by the Hong Kong Deposit Protection Board. Since 1 October 2024 eligible deposits are protected up to HK$800,000 per depositor per member bank. Some products, such as structured deposits and time deposits over five years, are not protected. Members must make prescribed statements about their membership and about whether each product is protected, and since 1 January 2025 must display the membership sign on e-banking platforms.
provisions.counselNote: Every product launch needs a DPS protection status and the right disclosure. Payout readiness also depends on data quality, such as accurate depositor records and aggregation across accounts.

provisions.title: The six data protection principles
provisions.summary: DPP1 governs the purpose and manner of collection and requires notice to the data subject. DPP2 covers accuracy and retention, DPP3 limits use to the original or a directly related purpose unless the data subject gives prescribed consent, DPP4 requires security, DPP5 requires openness and DPP6 gives a right of access and correction. Data users must use contractual or other means to bind their data processors on retention and security.
provisions.counselNote: Every outsourced cloud, eKYC and analytics vendor engages DPP2 and DPP4. As at May 2026 there was still no mandatory breach notification; reform was under study.

provisions.title: Direct marketing
provisions.summary: Before using personal data in direct marketing, a data user must tell the data subject of the intended use, the kinds of data and the classes of marketing subjects, and obtain consent. The data subject can opt out at any time. Giving data to third parties for their marketing needs a separate written consent. Breaches are criminal offences, with heavier penalties where data are provided for gain.
provisions.counselNote: Cross-selling through push notifications, in-app banners and partner offers is all caught. Unbundled consent and opt-outs that reach every downstream system are essential.

provisions.instrument: Code of Practice on Consumer Credit Data (PCPD)
provisions.ref: Code issued under the PDPO; read with HKMA SPM IC-6
provisions.title: Credit reference data and the multiple CRA model
provisions.summary: Governs what consumer credit data lenders may contribute to and obtain from credit reference agencies, how long the data may be kept, and the data subject's access rights. Under the multiple credit reference agency model ('Credit Data Smart', in full service since 26 April 2024), data flow through the industry Credit Reference Platform to the selected CRAs. HKMA SPM module IC-6 sets out what the HKMA expects of AIs.
provisions.counselNote: Lending products such as cards and personal loans depend on lawful contribution of credit data and lawful credit checks. Check consent wording, data access logging and dispute handling against the Code and IC-6.

provisions.instrument: Tournier v National Provincial and Union Bank of England
provisions.title: Banker's duty of confidentiality
provisions.summary: A bank owes an implied contractual duty not to disclose customer information. There are four exceptions: disclosure compelled by law, a duty to the public, the bank's own interests, and the customer's express or implied consent. Hong Kong courts apply it, and the Banking Ordinance contains no general bank-secrecy provision.
provisions.counselNote: Every disclosure (police production orders, JFIU, FINEST, group sharing, vendors) needs a Tournier exception as well as a PDPO basis. Keep a register of disclosures recording both.

provisions.title: Reasonableness of exclusion clauses
provisions.summary: Liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence cannot be excluded. Other exclusions of negligence liability, and exclusions in contracts where the other party deals as consumer or on the bank's written standard terms, are effective only if they pass the reasonableness test. The Unconscionable Contracts Ordinance (Cap. 458) separately allows a court to refuse to enforce unconscionable consumer contracts.
provisions.counselNote: Clickwrap terms are written standard terms. Clauses that put fraud or system-failure losses on the customer may fail the reasonableness test and will also be read against the Code of Banking Practice.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission
provisions.title: Suitability
provisions.summary: Using what it knows or should know about the client through due diligence, a licensed or registered person must ensure that any recommendation or solicitation is reasonably suitable for the client in all the circumstances. AIs that carry on regulated activities do so as registered institutions under the SFO, with the HKMA as frontline supervisor.
provisions.counselNote: Any fund marketplace or wealth feature in the app brings the suitability obligation, the mandatory suitability clause in client agreements, and the SFC's guidelines on online distribution and advisory platforms.

checklist: **Map the Code of Banking Practice** (December 2023 revision) clause by clause to app journeys, notifications and the terms and conditions, and track any gaps to closure.
**Write a playbook for unauthorised-transaction claims** covering the evidence needed to show gross negligence, refund timing, log preservation and escalation to complaints and the FDRC.

**Check that the DPS membership sign appears** on every e-banking screen where required, and that each product carries a protection status and any negative disclosure taken from a single product master record.
**Audit direct-marketing consent capture** under PDPO Part 6A: notice content, unbundled consents, separate consent for transfers to third parties, and how quickly opt-outs reach every system.
**Keep a register of confidential-data disclosures** recording the Tournier exception and the PDPO basis for each (JFIU, police orders, Part XIIAA sharing, CRAs, vendors).
**Review standard terms** under CECO and the Unconscionable Contracts Ordinance, and remove or narrow exclusions unlikely to pass the reasonableness test.
**Set service levels** for complaint acknowledgement and final response, and put signposting to the FDRC and HKMA in the app.
**Confirm the scope of the bank's SFO registration and insurance licensing** before any wealth, fund or insurance feature (including referral features) goes live.
itAngle: **Dispute evidence:** Build evidence for disputes: keep authentication events, device IDs and binding history, IP and session data, and the exact screens shown. Gross negligence has to be proved, and logs are the proof.

**Proof of acceptance:** Version-control every set of terms and every disclosure. Hash and timestamp each accepted version. The Electronic Transactions Ordinance (Cap. 553) gives electronic records and contracts legal effect, but the bank still has to prove what the customer actually saw.

**Marketing consents:** Treat consent management as code. PDPO Part 6A consents and opt-outs must reach the CRM, push-notification and marketing tools in near real time, with automated tests that block sends to customers who have opted out.
**Product master data:** Generate DPS signs, protection labels and risk disclosures from product master data rather than hard-coded copy, so that a product change automatically updates every channel.
virtualBankNotes: **Minimum balances:** The digital bank guideline says these banks should not impose any minimum account balance requirement or low-balance fees on customers, as part of their role in promoting financial inclusion (para 6).

**Remote channels:** With no branches, complaint handling, lost-device reporting and fraud-response channels must work entirely remotely and quickly. A 24/7 app creates an expectation of 24/7 response to scam reports.

**Vulnerable customers:** Vulnerable and elderly customers lack a branch fallback. Design assisted digital routes and friction for unusual transactions instead of relying on branch staff to spot problems.
**Digital disclosures:** Every disclosure is digital, so the bank must be able to prove that each one was presented and acknowledged, not merely published.
pitfalls: **Code as optional:** Treating the Code of Banking Practice as optional because it describes itself as voluntary. The HKMA supervises against it.
**Loss shifting:** Relying on terms and conditions to shift scam or unauthorised-transaction losses to customers without evidence of fraud or gross negligence.
**Bundled consent:** Bundling marketing consent with account opening, pre-ticking consent boxes, or sharing data with partners for their own marketing without separate written consent.
**Referral features:** Launching 'referral' or 'marketplace' features for funds or insurance without checking whether they amount to regulated dealing, advising or insurance distribution.

glossary.definition: Non-statutory code issued jointly by HKAB and the DTC Association and endorsed by the HKMA. It sets minimum standards for AIs' dealings with personal customers, and the HKMA monitors compliance as part of supervision.
Treat Customers Fairly. The HKMA's charter of five high-level principles for fair treatment of retail customers, signed by the retail banks in October 2013.

Financial Dispute Resolution Centre. It runs the Financial Dispute Resolution Scheme, which resolves monetary disputes between eligible customers and member financial institutions through mediation and then arbitration.
Deposit Protection Scheme under Cap. 581, administered by the Hong Kong Deposit Protection Board. It protects eligible deposits up to HK$800,000 per depositor per member bank from 1 October 2024.
The statement a Scheme member must make that a financial product (for example a structured deposit) is not a protected deposit under the DPS.

Brand name of Hong Kong's multiple credit reference agency model. Since April 2024, consumer credit data have flowed through an industry Credit Reference Platform to several selected CRAs instead of a single agency.
An authorized institution registered under the SFO to carry on regulated activities such as dealing in or advising on securities. The HKMA acts as its frontline supervisor.

The banker's implied contractual duty of confidentiality from Tournier [1924] 1 KB 461. It has four exceptions: compulsion of law, a duty to the public, the bank's own interests, and customer consent.

title: Supervision & enforcement
oneLiner: Most HKMA pressure is private and continuous; knowing the statutory powers behind it shapes every regulatory conversation.
keyPoints: Authorization starts the relationship with the HKMA; it does not end it. The HKMA supervises continuously and on a risk basis.

**Methods:** It rates every institution under its [[CAMEL rating]] system, combines off-site review of returns and management information with [[on-site examinations|on-site examination]] and thematic reviews, and meets boards, management and auditors regularly.

**Banking Ordinance:** gives the Monetary Authority (MA) information and inspection powers, a ladder of intervention powers for when things go wrong (directions, an [[Advisor]], a [[Manager]], suspension, revocation) and criminal offences for serious misconduct.
**AMLO:** The Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance adds a separate disciplinary regime with fines.
**Secrecy:** Statutory secrecy keeps most supervisory dealings private, so the enforcement the public sees is only a small part of the picture.
**Counsel's role:** Keep the relationship candid, timely and well documented.

deepDive.heading: Continuous, risk-based supervision
deepDive.lede: Supervision is continuous and mostly private.
points: **SA-1:** The HKMA assesses eight inherent risks and the quality of risk management, and integrates the results with its CAMEL rating.
**Supervisory intensity:** The rating sets how intensively the bank is supervised.

**Supervisory cycle:** Off-site analysis alternates with full-scope or thematic examinations, prudential meetings with management, and [[tripartite meetings|tripartite meeting]] with the external auditor.
**Confidentiality:** Ratings and findings are confidential supervisory information, so ask for the HKMA's view before repeating them to investors, parents or vendors.

deepDive.heading: Information and examination powers
deepDive.lede: The hard powers sit in the Ordinance.
points: **s.63:** underpins returns and ad hoc information requests.
**s.55:** underpins examinations.
**Section 59 reports:** under s.59(2) the MA can require a report from an auditor it has approved under s.59(3) (a [[section 59 report]]), the HKMA's equivalent of a skilled-person review.
**Auditor channels:** The bank's own auditor also has statutory reporting channels to the MA, so align with the auditor early.
**False information:** Individuals who give the MA materially false information can be prosecuted.

deepDive.heading: Escalation and appeals
deepDive.lede: Escalation usually starts with a findings letter and a remediation plan with deadlines.
points: **Directions and appointments:** Beyond that, s.52 lets the MA direct specific action, require the bank to consult an Advisor, or appoint a Manager.
**End points:** revocation (s.22, on [[Eighth Schedule]] grounds, after notice and a hearing under s.23) and suspension (ss.24–25).
**Appeals:** Appeals against many MA decisions go to the Chief Executive in Council; capital, liquidity and disclosure decisions go to the [[Banking Review Tribunal]].
**AML track:** AML breaches follow a separate track: under AMLO s.21 the HKMA can issue public reprimands, remedial orders and fines.
**Published enforcement:** This is where most published HKMA enforcement appears.

items.label: Findings letter
items.note: With a remediation plan and deadlines

items.label: s.52 powers
items.note: Direct specific action, require an Advisor, or appoint a Manager

items.label: Revocation or suspension
items.note: Revocation on Eighth Schedule grounds, after notice and a hearing

deepDive.heading: Working with the HKMA
deepDive.lede: For counsel, 'no surprises' is the working rule.
points: **Early reporting:** Report significant incidents and breaches early, with the known facts and a plan, and confirm every oral briefing in writing.
**Investigations:** Commission investigations through counsel, and give the HKMA facts, chronology and remediation rather than legal advice.
**Privileged reports:** If one must be produced, use express limited-waiver terms, accepting that protection against third parties is not guaranteed.
**s.120:** binds the HKMA, not the bank. It keeps supervisory files out of public view but does not make the bank's own documents privileged.
deepDive.takeaway: Contest examination findings on the facts, in writing, before the report is finalised.

provisions.title: Risk-based supervisory approach and CAMEL
provisions.summary: Describes the HKMA's risk-based supervision (V.2, 23 December 2022). It assesses eight types of inherent risk (credit, market, interest rate, liquidity, operational, reputation, legal and strategic) and the quality of risk management, integrates the results with the CAMEL rating system, and runs a cycle of off-site reviews, on-site examinations and meetings with the institution. The 2022 revision expects emerging risks, such as climate risk, to be considered within the eight inherent risks.
provisions.counselNote: This module explains why the HKMA asks what it asks. The CAMEL composite rating drives how intensively the bank is supervised and is confidential supervisory information.

provisions.title: Returns and information to the MA
provisions.summary: Requires AIs to submit periodic returns to the MA. s.63(2) also supports requests for further information the MA reasonably needs (HKMA forms such as the annual compliance certificate cite it as their legal basis). Non-compliance carries criminal sanctions.
provisions.counselNote: Every regulatory return and ad hoc HKMA data request rests on this section. Errors in returns are regulatory events in their own right, so treat their accuracy and sign-off controls as legal controls.

provisions.title: Examination of AIs
provisions.summary: Empowers the MA to examine an AI's books, accounts and transactions. The HKMA relies on this power for on-site examinations and thematic reviews, and information obtained this way is protected by statutory secrecy.
provisions.counselNote: Requests made during an examination are compulsory, not voluntary. Manage document production, interviews and responses to draft findings as you would a formal regulatory process.

provisions.title: Auditor reports required by the MA
provisions.summary: Under s.59(2) the MA may by notice require an AI to submit a report by an auditor on matters the MA reasonably requires for its functions; under s.59(3) the auditor must be approved by the MA. Published examples include reports on Bank of China (Hong Kong) in 2003 and Octopus Cards Limited in 2010.
provisions.counselNote: A s.59 report is the HKMA's 'skilled person' tool, often used after incidents or to validate remediation. Negotiate the scope and terms of reference carefully, because the report goes to the regulator. Separately, the bank's own auditor has statutory duties to report certain significant matters to the MA.

provisions.title: Remedial powers: directions, Advisor, Manager
provisions.summary: On statutory grounds that broadly cover actual or likely inability to meet obligations, conduct detrimental to depositors' interests and contraventions of the Ordinance, the MA may direct an AI to take specified action (s.52(1)(A)), require it to seek advice from an Advisor (s.52(1)(B)), or place the management of its affairs, business and property with a Manager (s.52(1)(C)).
provisions.counselNote: These are the HKMA's main intervention tools short of revocation; past examples include an Advisor direction for Octopus Cards Limited and a Manager for Delta Asia Credit Limited. Directions restricting new business or requiring management changes are the realistic escalation for a struggling digital bank.

provisions.title: Revocation, suspension and appeals
provisions.summary: s.22 allows the MA to revoke an authorization on grounds listed in the Eighth Schedule, after informing the AI of the grounds and giving it an opportunity to be heard (s.23). s.24 provides for temporary suspension and s.25 for suspension. s.132A provides appeals to the Chief Executive in Council against specified MA decisions; decisions on capital, liquidity and disclosure requirements are instead reviewable by the Banking Review Tribunal.
provisions.counselNote: Revocation is the last resort, but its grounds (the HKMA treats the authorization criteria as continuing to apply after authorization) frame every serious supervisory conversation. Diarise appeal time limits as soon as any adverse decision is notified.

provisions.title: Official secrecy
provisions.summary: Prohibits the MA and persons performing functions under the Ordinance from disclosing information about any person's affairs obtained in that capacity, subject to listed exceptions (gateways) such as disclosure to other regulators in defined circumstances.
provisions.counselNote: This explains why the HKMA will not discuss peers and why examination reports are not public. It binds the HKMA, not the bank, and does not make the bank's own documents privileged.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Disciplinary action by relevant authorities
provisions.summary: Where a financial institution contravenes specified requirements (including the Schedule 2 customer due diligence and record-keeping requirements), the relevant authority, which for AIs is the HKMA, may publicly reprimand it, order remedial action, and impose a pecuniary penalty of up to the greater of HK$10 million or three times the profit gained or costs avoided.
provisions.counselNote: Most of the HKMA's public enforcement actions against banks are taken under this power. Read the HKMA's published guideline on exercising the pecuniary penalty power for the factors that aggravate or mitigate a penalty.

provisions.title: Criminal offences counsel should know
provisions.summary: Offences include issuing deposit advertisements other than by an AI, subject to exceptions (s.92), using 'bank' in a name without being a licensed bank or the MA's consent (s.97), holding out as a bank (s.97A), staff making false entries in an AI's records (s.123), and directors or employees accepting advantages for showing favour in granting credit (s.124). The Ordinance also penalises producing information that is false in a material particular; in January 2009 the District Court fined individuals for Banking Ordinance offences including this one.
provisions.counselNote: ss.123 and 124 apply to staff conduct and belong in training and the code of conduct. The false-information offences matter personally for anyone who signs returns or HKMA responses.

provisions.instrument: HKMA circular: Management Accountability at Registered Institutions
provisions.title: Senior management accountability (MIC-aligned)
provisions.summary: Sets HKMA expectations, in FAQ form, for senior management accountability over securities (regulated) activities at registered institutions, aligned with the SFC's Manager-in-Charge regime. 'Management' covers chief executives, alternate chief executives, directors approved under s.71 of the Banking Ordinance, managers under s.72B, executive officers approved under s.71C, and other persons involved in management.
provisions.counselNote: This becomes relevant if the digital bank registers to distribute investment products. Map responsible individuals and reporting lines, and keep s.71 approvals, s.72B manager notifications and executive officer approvals current.

checklist: **Map every regulatory return** to its data sources, owner and sign-off, and treat return errors as reportable events.
**Set up a single regulatory correspondence log** and point-of-contact protocol so that every HKMA request and response passes through legal or compliance.
**Prepare an examination playbook** covering a document request tracker, interviewee briefings and a factual-accuracy review step for draft findings.
**Agree a board-approved self-reporting policy** with thresholds, timelines and decision owners ('no surprises').
**Track every HKMA finding to closure** with root cause, owner, deadline and evidence, and report progress to the board.
**Protect privilege** by engaging investigators through counsel, separating factual chronologies from legal advice, and using limited-waiver terms when production is unavoidable.
**Brief approved individuals** (chief executive, alternate chief executives, directors and any executive officers) on their personal exposure under the Banking Ordinance and AMLO.
**Negotiate the terms of reference** for any s.59 engagement, covering scope, access, timetable and the bank's opportunity to comment on the draft report.
itAngle: **Data lineage:** Regulatory returns are data pipelines. Errors in source systems, transformations or reporting logic become s.63 issues, so data lineage, reconciliations and change control over reporting code are compliance controls.

**System evidence:** Examinations increasingly ask for system evidence such as access logs, configuration baselines, change tickets and test results. Keep it quickly retrievable, as you would for e-discovery.

**Supervisory confidentiality:** Classify HKMA correspondence and findings as restricted. Limit access in document systems, and check that collaboration or AI tools do not send confidential supervisory material to third-party services without assessment.
virtualBankNotes: **Business plan:** Expect the HKMA to compare actual performance with the business plan submitted at authorization. Discuss material changes to products, partners or growth before they happen.

**Exit plan:** The digital bank guideline requires an exit plan for an orderly unwind if the business model fails (para 20). Keep it current, because persistent losses or capital pressure will bring it into supervisory discussion.

**Incident visibility:** Technology incidents at a digital bank are visible to customers and the HKMA immediately, so incident reporting is a frequent contact point with the supervisor and a real test of 'no surprises'.

**Securities business:** If the bank distributes investment products as a registered institution, the management accountability and conduct expectations for securities business add another supervisory layer.
pitfalls: **Sharing ratings:** Repeating CAMEL ratings or examination findings to investors, parents or vendors without first consulting the HKMA.
**Late disclosure:** Letting the HKMA learn of a problem from the media or the auditor before hearing it from the bank.
**Privilege waiver:** Producing privileged investigation reports without considering waiver consequences or recording the terms of production.
**Adversarial or informal:** Treating the HKMA like an opposing litigant (adversarial, over-lawyered responses), or the opposite: relying on informal oral understandings with no written record.

glossary.definition: The HKMA's composite supervisory rating covering Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings and Liquidity, assigned on a five-point scale. It sets supervisory intensity and is confidential.
An HKMA inspection of an institution's records, systems and staff, either full-scope or thematic, carried out under the MA's examination powers.
A meeting between the HKMA, the institution and its external auditor to discuss audit and supervisory findings.

A report the MA requires an institution, by notice under s.59(2), to obtain from an MA-approved auditor on matters the MA specifies. It is commonly used to investigate problems or validate remediation.
A person appointed by the MA whose advice an institution is required, under s.52, to seek on the management of its affairs.
A person appointed under s.52 to manage the affairs, business and property of an institution in place of its own management.
The Schedule to the Banking Ordinance listing the grounds on which the MA may revoke an authorization under s.22.

A statutory tribunal, chaired by a person qualified for appointment as a High Court judge, that reviews MA decisions on capital, liquidity and disclosure requirements. It was originally established as the Capital Adequacy Review Tribunal.

title: Recovery & resolution
oneLiner: If the bank fails, contract terms, exit triggers and payout readiness decide whether depositors are paid in an orderly way.
keyPoints: This area covers what happens as a bank moves from stress to failure. It has three layers.

**First, the bank:** its own preparation, a [[recovery plan]] under SPM RE-1 setting out actions it can take itself and, for a digital bank, an [[exit plan]] for an orderly wind-down that does not disrupt customers or the financial system.
**Second, HKMA powers:** its supervisory powers under the Banking Ordinance allow it to give directions or appoint an Advisor or Manager without formal resolution.

**Third, FIRO:** The Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance (Cap. 628) makes the HKMA the resolution authority for banks. Where a bank's failure would threaten financial stability, it can override shareholders, creditors and counterparties.
**Deposit protection:** Alongside these, the Deposit Protection Scheme (Cap. 581) pays insured depositors quickly if a bank is simply liquidated.
**Realistic end-states:** For a small digital bank, a solvent wind-down or liquidation with a DPS payout, rather than bail-in.

deepDive.heading: Recovery planning under RE-1
deepDive.lede: Start with the escalation ladder. Recovery is led by the bank.
points: **RE-1:** a statutory guideline, revised in 2020.
**Board-owned plan:** It expects a board-owned plan with quantitative and qualitative triggers set above regulatory minimums, credible and tested options, and a communications plan.
**2020 revision:** added triggers such as a rapid fall in profitability and major operational incidents, both relevant to a tech-dependent bank.

items.label: Recovery
items.note: Led by the bank: board-owned plan, triggers set above minimums

items.label: Supervisory action
items.note: Directions, an Advisor or a Manager

items.label: Resolution or liquidation
items.note: FIRO only if non-viable and a threat to financial stability; otherwise court liquidation

deepDive.heading: Supervisory action and liquidation
deepDive.lede: If recovery fails, the MA can act under s.52 of the Banking Ordinance.
points: **Advisor or Manager:** It can direct the bank, appoint an Advisor or, after consulting the Financial Secretary, appoint a Manager to run the business.
**Small banks:** For a small bank these remain the main tools.
**Liquidation:** then proceeds through the court under Cap. 32, with the DPS paying protected depositors up to HK$800,000 each, against a seven-day payout target.

deepDive.heading: FIRO resolution conditions
deepDive.lede: FIRO is reserved for cases that meet the s.25 conditions.
points: **Non-viability:** The bank must have ceased, or be likely to cease, to be viable, with no reasonable prospect of private-sector action restoring viability.
**Systemic risk:** Its failure must also threaten Hong Kong's financial stability, including the continuity of [[critical financial functions]].
deepDive.takeaway: Without that systemic risk, resolution is not available.

deepDive.heading: Stabilization options
points: **Five options:** transfer to a purchaser, transfer to a [[bridge institution]], transfer to an asset management vehicle, [[bail-in]] and transfer to a temporary public ownership company.
