deepDive.heading: LAC, stays and netting
points: **Resolution entities:** [[LAC]] requirements (Cap. 628B) apply only to AIs the HKMA classifies as resolution entities (or their material subsidiaries): in practice the larger banks.
**Classification criteria:** Confirm the current classification criteria with the HKMA.
**Smaller banks:** Two FIRO regimes can still reach a smaller bank.
**Cap. 628C:** The Stay Rules require a [[contractual stay]] term in non-Hong Kong-law financial contracts, recognising the HKMA's power under s.90 to suspend termination rights.
**Cap. 628A:** The Protected Arrangements Regulation governs how set-off, netting and security survive partial transfers.

deepDive.heading: Counsel's contractual levers
deepDive.lede: Counsel's main lever is contractual.
points: **Vendors:** Core banking, cloud, payments and KYC vendors should not be able to terminate or suspend service because of recovery action, an HKMA direction, a s.52 Manager or resolution, provided they are paid.
**Transfer and exit:** They should also support transfer and exit.
**Exit plan:** Align exit-plan triggers with recovery triggers.
**Parent support:** Make the parent's commitment to fund depositor repayment legally binding.

provisions.title: Conditions for initiating resolution
provisions.summary: Resolution may be initiated only if the institution has ceased, or is likely to cease, to be viable, with no reasonable prospect of private-sector action restoring viability. Its non-viability must also pose risks to the stability and effective working of Hong Kong's financial system, including the continued performance of critical financial functions.
provisions.counselNote: For a small digital bank the systemic-risk limb may not be met, which points to insolvency plus a DPS payout rather than FIRO tools. Plan for both paths.

provisions.title: The five stabilization options
provisions.summary: FIRO gives the HKMA, as resolution authority for banking sector entities, five options: transfer to a purchaser, transfer to a bridge institution, transfer to an asset management vehicle, statutory bail-in, and transfer to a temporary public ownership company. FIRO commenced on 7 July 2017.
provisions.counselNote: Transfer-based options only work if contracts, licences and data can follow the business to a new owner. Assignment and novation clauses in key contracts should allow this.

provisions.title: No creditor worse off
provisions.summary: Pre-resolution shareholders and creditors are entitled to compensation if an independent valuation shows they fared worse in resolution than they would have in a hypothetical winding up of the institution.
provisions.counselNote: The comparison is with insolvency, so creditor ranking and set-off positions in a winding up matter even in resolution. Keep the bank's creditor hierarchy analysis current.

provisions.title: MA's powers over a troubled AI
provisions.summary: In defined circumstances, such as an AI likely to be unable to meet its obligations or conducting business in a manner detrimental to depositors, the MA may give directions (s.52(1)(A)) or appoint a Manager to run the AI's affairs, business and property (s.52(1)(C), after consulting the Financial Secretary). The MA may also appoint an Advisor. A Manager's appointment can later be revoked under s.53F.
provisions.counselNote: These are the likeliest intervention tools for a small bank. Check that the insolvency-event definitions in vendor and funding contracts do not treat a s.52 appointment as a termination trigger.

provisions.title: Recovery planning
provisions.summary: A statutory guideline under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance. It requires AIs to maintain board-approved recovery plans with calibrated triggers, stress scenarios, credible recovery options assessed for feasibility and impact, and communication plans, assuming no public support beyond eligibility for HKMA liquidity facilities.
provisions.counselNote: Counsel should check the governance (who can invoke the plan, board approval, annual review) and the legal feasibility of each option, for example whether assets can be sold or a capital raise made quickly.

provisions.instrument: Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks (s.16(10))
provisions.title: Exit plan for a failed business model
provisions.summary: The guideline requires a digital bank applicant to provide an exit plan in case its business model turns out to be unsuccessful, so that the bank can unwind its business operations in an orderly manner without disrupting customers or the financial system. The plan should cover the circumstances that trigger it, the authority to trigger it, the channels for repaying depositors and the source of funding for those payments.
provisions.counselNote: This is a live obligation, not a one-off licensing document. Its triggers should be built into the board's risk appetite and tested alongside the recovery plan.

provisions.title: Deposit Protection Scheme
provisions.summary: Licensed banks are Scheme members unless exempted. Protected deposits are covered up to HK$800,000 per depositor per member bank from 1 October 2024. The Deposit Protection Board targets payout within seven days on a gross basis. Structured deposits, time deposits with an original term over five years, bearer instruments and offshore deposits are not protected.
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank is a Scheme member. Counsel should check product labelling and the DPS membership representations in the app, and the bank's ability to produce depositor data for a fast payout.

provisions.instrument: Financial Institutions (Resolution) (Contractual Recognition of Suspension of Termination Rights - Banking Sector) Rules (Cap. 628C)
provisions.ref: Stay Rules; Code of Practice ST-1
provisions.title: Contractual recognition of resolution stays
provisions.summary: These Rules were made under s.92 of FIRO and came into force on 27 August 2021. Covered entities (Hong Kong-incorporated AIs and certain group companies) must include, in covered financial contracts governed by non-Hong Kong law, a term by which the counterparty agrees to be bound by a suspension of termination rights under s.90 of FIRO (up to two business days). Code of Practice chapter ST-1 explains how the HKMA will exercise its discretions under the Rules.
provisions.counselNote: Inventory any ISDA, GMRA or similar foreign-law contracts and confirm that the stay language or protocol adherence is in place. Technology contracts are not 'financial contracts', so continuity for them depends on drafting.

provisions.title: Operational continuity in resolution
provisions.summary: Issued by the HKMA as resolution authority. It sets expectations for ex-ante arrangements so that critical financial functions and the essential services supporting them, including intra-group and third-party services, can continue during and after resolution. It is read with RA-2 (approach to resolution planning) and CI-1 (core information requirements).
provisions.counselNote: Even where formal resolution planning for the bank is light, OCIR-1 is the best benchmark for resolution-resilient clauses in outsourcing, cloud and intra-group service agreements.

provisions.instrument: Financial Institutions (Resolution) (Loss-absorbing Capacity Requirements - Banking Sector) Rules (Cap. 628B)
provisions.title: Loss-absorbing capacity requirements
provisions.summary: These Rules were made under s.19(1) of FIRO and came into operation on 14 December 2018. They require AIs that the MA classifies as resolution entities, or as material subsidiaries of them, to hold minimum LAC. In practice they reach the larger banks rather than small digital banks; the HKMA decides the classification.
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank is unlikely to be in scope. Confirm this with the HKMA rather than assume it, and keep it under review if the bank grows or is acquired by a larger group.

checklist: **Map critical vendors** (core banking, cloud, payments, card processing, KYC and the parent's shared platforms) and review their termination, suspension and change-of-control triggers. Carve out HKMA directions, s.52 appointments, recovery actions and resolution.

**Negotiate resolution-resilience terms**: continued service while fees are paid, assignment or novation to a purchaser or bridge institution, exit assistance, data return in a usable format, and access to configuration and keys.
**Inventory non-Hong Kong-law financial contracts** and confirm compliance with the Stay Rules, through bespoke clauses or ISDA/ICMA protocol adherence.
**Audit recovery plan governance**: board approval, annual refresh, trigger calibration against the capital and liquidity plan, the escalation chain, and evidence of dry runs.
**Write exit-plan triggers** into the risk appetite statement (for example CET1 runway, losses against plan, missed parent funding milestones) and document who can invoke the plan.
**Make the parent's funding commitment** for depositor repayment and wind-down costs legally enforceable, and test whether it is still credible.
**Verify DPS readiness**: correct protected and non-protected product labelling, membership representations in app and web journeys, and depositor data quality for payout files.
**Prepare an intervention playbook** covering HKMA liaison, board convening, privilege, customer communications, staff retention and preservation of records.
itAngle: **Stack separation:** Operational continuity is an architecture question. Can the bank's stack be separated from the group and handed to a purchaser or bridge institution while the legal owner changes? Shared parent platforms and group-owned cloud tenancies are the usual blockers.

**Exit execution:** Executing an exit plan is a large data-migration and payments project. It needs verified payee details, bulk FPS or transfer repayments, account-closure workflows, mass customer notification and retention of records after the bank ceases business.

**Payout data:** A DPS payout depends on producing accurate depositor-level, aggregated data in the format the Deposit Protection Board prescribes. Treat it as a tested 'single customer view' export, not a one-off script.

**Operational controls:** Continuity clauses only work if the operational controls match: API credentials, encryption keys, admin accounts and data should sit in tenancies the bank controls, with runbooks for vendor exit and handover.
virtualBankNotes: **Exit plan:** The digital bank guideline requires an exit plan covering the triggers, who can trigger it, the depositor repayment channels and the source of funds (para 20). For a loss-making bank this is the most important resolution-related document.
**DPS membership:** As licensed banks, digital banks are DPS members, so protected deposits are covered up to HK$800,000 per depositor.

**Failure paths:** A small digital bank is unlikely to be a LAC resolution entity. Its realistic failure paths are solvent wind-down, a sale or a s.52 Manager, followed by liquidation and a DPS payout.
**Contractual continuity:** Heavy reliance on group platforms and cloud makes contractual continuity critical, even if the HKMA does not require full resolution planning.
pitfalls: **Licensing-stage exit plan:** Treating the exit plan as a licensing-stage document rather than a live plan with calibrated triggers, a named decision-maker and committed funding.

**Insolvency event clauses:** Leaving vendor 'insolvency event' clauses broad enough to catch a regulatory direction, a s.52 Manager or resolution, which hands the vendor a walk-away right at the worst moment.
**Stay Rules scope:** Assuming the Stay Rules protect technology and outsourcing contracts. They target non-Hong Kong-law financial contracts.
**Mislabelled products:** Mislabelling products as deposit-protected (for example structured deposits or long-term time deposits), which creates misrepresentation and DPS compliance issues.

glossary.definition: A bank-owned plan of actions to restore its viability under severe stress without public support beyond normal central bank facilities, with triggers, options and governance (SPM RE-1).
A digital bank's plan for unwinding its business in an orderly way if its business model fails. It covers triggers, who can trigger it, how depositors are repaid and how that repayment is funded.
A stabilization option under which the resolution authority writes down liabilities or converts them into equity to recapitalise a failing institution, without taxpayer funding.
A temporary entity controlled by the resolution authority that takes over critical business from a failing institution so that it can continue until it is sold or wound down.
No creditor worse off: the safeguard by which shareholders and creditors are compensated if resolution leaves them worse off than a hypothetical winding up would have done.

Loss-absorbing capacity: capital and eligible debt that can be written down or converted to absorb losses and recapitalise a bank in resolution. In Hong Kong it is set by Cap. 628B for AIs the HKMA classifies as resolution entities.

A contract term by which a counterparty agrees to be bound by the resolution authority's temporary suspension of its termination rights. It is needed because foreign courts might not otherwise recognise the statutory stay.
Activities, such as deposit-taking and payments, whose sudden discontinuation would be likely to disrupt the financial system or the economy. Their protection is a central objective of resolution.
